title: Fraud and misrepresentation: editorial notes and questions
summary: Read the surrounding notes and questions alongside the principal cases. The complete assigned pages are preserved here.
notes:
Swinton v. Whitinsville Savings Bank: It establishes the baseline that Kannavos qualifies: silence, a half-truth, active concealment, and a special duty to speak are different grounds of analysis.

Kannavos v. Annino: It shows how individually true statements become deceptive in context and how a duty to complete a partial disclosure differs from a duty to volunteer all information.

Speakers of Sport v. ProServ: It helps distinguish a legally assumed risk, an optimistic prediction, and a promise made with fraudulent intent.

Vokes v. Arthur Murray, Inc.: It demonstrates how the speaker’s expertise and the surrounding sales process can change the legal significance of apparently subjective praise.

Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp.: This case links fraud, interpretation, signed releases, and assent. Its result depends on the disclaimer’s specificity and the courts’ account of available precautions.
